question: While a collection is being indexed for the first time, does the mount's view of a file that an application already has open change under it -- enough for the desktop to tell the application the file was modified?
why_now: Observed once, by the account owner, on the Arch VM on 2026-09-15, minutes after signing in and while the linked SharePoint library was still on its first index pass. They opened a 25 MB text file from the mount in GNOME Text Editor, typed nothing, closed it, and were asked "Save Changes? Open documents contain unsaved changes. Changes which are not saved will be permanently lost." The editor had marked the document modified on its own.

what_is_already_known.the_bytes_are_right: Read twice in full through the mount, the file gives the same SHA-256 (42dd1fe1...), 25,332,920 bytes, mtime unchanged, UTF-8, LF only, no NUL bytes, ending in a newline. A copy taken to local disk has the same hash. Nothing was corrupted and nothing could have been lost by discarding.
what_is_already_known.it_does_not_reproduce_after_indexing: With both feeds ready, the same file opened from the mount and the same file opened from a local copy, both launched from a command line and closed with ctrl-w after thirty seconds, close with no prompt and no modified marker in the title.
what_is_already_known.the_desktop_sees_no_difference_now: gio info on the mounted file and on the local copy agree on content type, size, mode and writability; unix::blocks differ by one, which is the last block rounding.
what_is_already_known.metadata_is_stable_now: stat on two files twenty-five seconds apart: identical size, mtime and ctime.

hypothesis: The first index pass is the difference. Before an item is indexed the mount answers from what the provider says; afterwards it answers from the index. If any field the desktop watches -- modification time above all -- differs between those two answers, GIO's file monitor reports a change on a file an application has open, and the application marks its document dirty. That would make this a real defect with a narrow window: the first minutes of a new connection, which is exactly when a person is most likely to be opening things to see whether it worked.
the_alternative: The person typed a character without noticing. A VM window captures the keyboard, and a space is easy. This cannot be excluded after the fact and is why the run below has to be done rather than argued about.
how_to_test: On a VM with an account, stop the daemon, move the account's metadata.db aside, start it again so the collection indexes from nothing. During the first pass: open a large file from the mount in GNOME Text Editor, touch nothing, and sample `stat` on that file every second. Then close the editor. The run answers three things: whether stat's mtime or size ever moves for a file that did not change in the cloud, whether the editor marks the document, and whether both happen at the same moment.

predictions.claim: The mount's mtime for the file changes at least once during the first index pass, without the file changing in the cloud.
predictions.role: the mechanism. If mtime never moves, the hypothesis is wrong and the editor's marker has another cause.

predictions.claim: The editor marks the document modified within a few seconds of that change, and asks to save on close.
predictions.role: the symptom, tied to the mechanism rather than to the clock

predictions.claim: The file's bytes are identical before and after, which is what makes this a wrong prompt rather than a loss.
predictions.role: discriminator -- if the bytes differ, this is a far more serious defect and stops being about a dialog

decision_rule: P1 and P2 together name a defect to fix: the mount must not change a file's observable metadata because its own index caught up. P1 failing means the cause is elsewhere and the observation stays open with one occurrence and no mechanism. P3 failing outranks everything here.
